title: George v. Commissioner
subject: Documentation Standards
summary: George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10) is a February 3, 2026 U.S. Tax Court ruling on IRC § 41 R&D tax credits flowing from a poultry S corporation. The court accepted broiler flocks as pilot models and supply-only QREs, but disallowed much of the claim for weak contemporaneous records and cut the ASC rate from 14% to 6%.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Context

On February 3, 2026, the United States Tax Court issued its memorandum opinion in Gary C. George and Robin A. George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10 (Docket Nos. 27494-16, 21889-21), authored by Judge Travis A. Greaves. Framing the central evidentiary conflict of the litigation, Judge Greaves opened the over-80-page opinion by asking: "Forget the proverbial chicken or the egg; today we are called to answer which came first, the research or the research credit study?". The ruling represents a watershed moment in federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41, establishing critical precedent governing applied commercial-scale experimentation, the treatment of biological assets as "pilot models" under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4), the fatal vulnerability of retrospective interview-based credit studies when contradicted by operational records, and the strict evidentiary threshold required to substantiate base-period Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC).

The petitioners, Gary C. George and his wife Robin A. George, reported research credits that flowed through from George's of Missouri, Inc. (GOMI), of which Gary C. George was the sole shareholder; GOMI was an S corporation operating as the live-production arm of one of the largest vertically integrated poultry processing conglomerates in the United States. Within the corporate structure, GOMI managed the hatcheries, live haul, feed mills, and grow-out farms (owned by independent contract growers who raised GOMI-owned flocks) responsible for raising "broilers" (chickens raised specifically for commercial meat processing and sale, as distinguished from "breeders" that lay eggs), while affiliated corporate entities executed post-grow-out processing and commercial distribution. Because commercial poultry production is a high-volume, low-margin industry, GOMI relied extensively on operational data analytics, nutritional chemistry, veterinary medicine, and genetic selection to improve feed conversion efficiency, mitigate avian disease pressures, and achieve uniform bird weights at slaughter.

GOMI did not claim IRC § 41 research credits on its originally filed federal income tax returns for taxable years 2012, 2013, and 2014. In 2014, following a referral from its longtime certified public accounting firm, Frost PLLC, George's (through an August 30, 2014 engagement letter signed on behalf of George's, Inc., and related entities, including GOMI) engaged the consulting firm alliantgroup to perform a retrospective R&D tax credit study covering the 2012 through 2014 tax years. After interviewing GOMI personnel and reviewing company files, the consulting firm produced two written reports totaling nearly 100 pages, and petitioners ultimately litigated seven "research trials" involving coccidiostat feed additives (Salinomycin), digestive enzymes (phytase), probiotics (Floramax, Sporulin, and Calsporin), vaccines and antibiotics (HatchPak, Tylan, Vaxxitek, and laryngotracheitis (LT) vaccines), and a broiler genetic line (Ross 708).

Relying on this retrospective study, GOMI filed amended returns claiming more than $4.4 million in federal research tax credits ($1,070,380 for 2012, $2,870,901 for 2013, and $530,317 for 2014, the last figure reflecting a reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c)) generated from approximately $63 million in claimed QREs ($16,450,745 for 2012, $29,478,367 for 2013, and $17,025,243 for 2014) across the three-year period, with substantial credit amounts carried forward to subsequent tax years. Notably, GOMI elected not to claim any qualified employee wage expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), concluding that the administrative burden of tracking and allocating employee time was not worth the effort. Instead, GOMI's claimed QREs consisted exclusively of qualified supply expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C)—specifically, the cost of the feed (including medications mixed into it, but excluding the shrink adjustment and allocated overhead) delivered to the broiler flocks raised on grower farms during the purported trial windows. To compute the credit, GOMI elected the ASC method under IRC § 41(c)(5).
The Internal Revenue Service Challenge

Following examinations and the denial of the Georges' individual refund claims, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the claimed research credits in their entirety and, in a July 15, 2021 notice of deficiency, asserted 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) for tax years 2014 and 2016 ($106,063 and $95,256, respectively), two of the taxable years in which the credits were utilized. The IRS mounted a comprehensive legal and factual assault against the claim; as the court framed the primary dispute, the question was whether GOMI actually conducted research trials during the research years or whether the alleged trials were "merely post hoc distortions of routine data collection into the model of section 41 qualified research". In the agency's view, GOMI's activities constituted ordinary commercial poultry production and routine quality control rather than intentional scientific experimentation. Furthermore, because the vaccines, probiotics, enzymes, and genetic lines were commercially available inputs that had already undergone laboratory testing by third-party vendors, the IRS argued that GOMI faced no genuine technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or design at the outset of its activities.

Beyond challenging the experimental nature of the trials, the IRS attacked GOMI's business component classification and cost eligibility. Invoking the product-versus-process distinction of IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Union Carbide Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012) (the opinion does not cite United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023)), the IRS asserted that GOMI's activities were directed at improving its production process—raising chickens more efficiently to reduce operating costs—rather than developing a product. Without addressing the pilot model argument, the IRS also maintained that the feed costs were not deductible under section 174 where the tested product was not administered in the feed (HatchPak was applied by spray and Floramax through drinking water), and further contended that GOMI's failure to claim wage QREs legally precluded it from claiming standalone supply QREs. Additionally, the IRS argued that any project aimed at controlling broiler uniformity, because GOMI must produce broilers of certain sizes to sell to customers, fell within the statutory exclusion for adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), and that the trials were excluded routine testing or quality control under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D). Finally, on an evidentiary level, the record showed that GOMI's contemporaneous feed recipes and settlement data either failed to corroborate or directly contradicted several of the experimental narratives, and the court ultimately held that petitioners' back-casted ratio estimate of the 2009–2011 base-period QREs had no evidentiary foundation, disqualifying GOMI from the 14% ASC rate.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

To adjudicate the deficiency notices, the Tax Court evaluated GOMI's activities under the interlocking provisions of IRC §§ 41, 174, 6001, and 6662. Under IRC § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer is allowed a credit equal to 20% of the excess of qualified research expenses for the taxable year over the base amount, or alternatively, under the ASC election of IRC § 41(c)(5)(A), a credit equal to 14% of so much of the QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years. However, pursuant to the start-up and unsubstantiated base limitation of IRC § 41(c)(5)(B), if a taxpayer has zero QREs—or fails to substantiate QREs—in any one of the three preceding taxable years, the ASC rate is statutorily reduced to 6% of current-year QREs.

For expenditures to constitute QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)—which encompasses in-house research wages under § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), with supplies defined in § 41(b)(2)(C) as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, or property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation—the underlying activity must satisfy the four-part statutory test of IRC § 41(d)(1) applied separately to each "business component". IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) defines a business component as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer.

The first element of the four-part test is the Section 174 Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), which requires that expenditures qualify as expenses collectible under IRC § 174. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1), research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense are expenditures incurred in activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of the product. Crucially, under the 2014 amendments to Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4), the costs of producing a "pilot model"—defined as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product, including a fully-functional representation or model—qualify as deductible § 174 research expenditures. Furthermore, taxpayers claiming the § 41 credit in coordination with § 174 (including the post-2021 amortization regime enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and, for domestic research expenditures in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, the deduction under IRC § 174A) must either reduce their deductible or amortizable research expenditures by the gross credit amount or make a reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c).

The second statutory requirement is the Technological Information Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), which mandates that research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Pursuant to Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4), this requires that the process of experimentation fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. The third requirement is the Business Component or Permitted Purpose Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), under which the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, specifically targeting a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, while excluding aesthetic or cosmetic alterations. The fourth requirement is the Process of Experimentation Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), which stipulates that substantially all (defined in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5), a process of experimentation is a systematic evaluative process consistent with the scientific method that is designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design of that result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities.

Even if an activity satisfies all four prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1), it must not fall within the eight statutory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4), which disallow credits for research conducted after the beginning of commercial production (§ 41(d)(4)(A)), adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (§ 41(d)(4)(B)), duplication of an existing business component (§ 41(d)(4)(C)), surveys and routine data collection or ordinary testing and inspection for quality control (§ 41(d)(4)(D)), and research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity (§ 41(d)(4)(H)). Finally, under IRC § 6001 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d), the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of maintaining contemporaneous records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit.
The Tax Court's Final Holding

In a nuanced, split decision that directed final deficiency and overpayment computations under Tax Court Rule 155, Judge Greaves delivered a major doctrinal victory for commercial-scale applied R&D while simultaneously decimating the dollar value of GOMI's claim due to pervasive substantiation failures. On the threshold legal questions, the Tax Court validated applied agricultural R&D and pilot model supply QREs, rejecting the IRS's argument that qualified research only occurs in sterile laboratories or that commercial farm trials are per se routine production. The court held that GOMI's business component was a product (an "improved poultry product"—specifically, a healthier, more uniform broiler) rather than a production process, and rejected the IRS's adaptation exclusion argument under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) because developing the new bird specifications involved a magnitude of change greater than minor alterations. Applying Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4), the court held that the experimental flocks of broilers were valid "pilot models" because biological uncertainty could only be resolved by raising the birds to end market weights under commercial production conditions. Consequently, the feed costs of qualifying experimental flocks constituted deductible § 174 pilot model expenditures and valid supply QREs under § 41(b)(2)(C), and the court affirmed that taxpayers have the flexibility to claim standalone supply QREs even when they elect to claim zero wage QREs.

When evaluating the seven trials on a project-by-project basis, however, the court enforced a strict evidentiary standard that prioritized contemporaneous operational records over the retrospective alliantgroup study. The court completely disallowed three of the seven trials (Salinomycin, Phytase, and Vaxxitek), partially disallowed three multi-faceted trials (HatchPak and Tylan, allowed for 2012 with $5,115,281 in QREs but disallowed for 2013; the probiotic trials, disallowed as to Floramax but allowed as to Sporulin and Calsporin with $4,748,616 and $2,531,962 in 2013 QREs; and LT Vaccines, disallowed as to method of administration but allowed as to 2014 vector priming for only six big broiler contracts with $1,521,039 in QREs), and allowed in full only the Ross 708 Genetic Line trial ($398,520 in 2014 QREs), for total allowed QREs of $5,115,281 for 2012, $7,280,578 for 2013, and $1,919,559 for 2014.

Compounding these project disallowances, the court rejected GOMI's unsubstantiated 10.23% ratio estimate for its 2009–2011 base-period QREs, holding that the common-law estimation rule of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930) cannot be invoked where the taxpayer offers no foundational evidence permitting an informed estimate. Because GOMI failed to substantiate its base period, the court applied the IRC § 41(c)(5)(B) start-up limitation, slashing GOMI's credit calculation rate from 14% to 6% and ultimately leaving the taxpayer with less than 20% of its originally claimed credits. Despite this substantial disallowance, the court fully abated the 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6664(c), holding that the petitioners acted with reasonable cause and in good faith by relying on a comprehensive study (two reports totaling nearly 100 pages) prepared by an experienced advisory firm that had been given open access to George's books, records, and employees.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The dramatic reduction imposed on GOMI's claim—cutting over $4.4 million in claimed credits down to less than 20% of that amount—did not stem from judicial hostility toward non-laboratory R&D, nor did it result from the nature of the agricultural industry. Rather, the disallowances were driven by six distinct legal, technical, and accounting deficiencies that arose when a retrospective consulting narrative collided with raw operational records.
Failure 1: Retroactive Narrative Reconstruction Contradicted by Contemporaneous Operational Logs ("The Chicken Before the Egg")

The most damaging evidentiary failure in George v. Commissioner occurred where the retrospective tax study constructed a narrative of systematic dosage experimentation based on employee memory interviews, only to be flatly refuted by GOMI's contemporaneous feed recipes. Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and (C), a taxpayer must establish that technical uncertainty existed at the outset of the project and that the taxpayer actually evaluated one or more alternatives to resolve that uncertainty.

In the Salinomycin coccidiostat trial and the Phytase enzyme trial (which petitioners tied to flocks under 12 and 232 contracts, respectively; the opinion does not quantify the QREs claimed for either), petitioners asserted that GOMI's consulting veterinarian and nutritionist, Dr. Fussel and Dr. Greenwood, tested higher Salinomycin dosages combined with chemical coccidiostats such as Robenz to improve coccidiosis control, and that Dr. Greenwood varied phytase dosages according to feed composition to develop a dosing matrix that would deliver the enzyme's promised cost savings. However, when the Tax Court examined GOMI's contemporaneous feed formulation recipes, the objective records showed that GOMI added the same dosages of Salinomycin as in prior years (with Robenz appearing in only a single April 3, 2012 grower recipe that petitioners could not connect to the remaining experimental flocks) and that every relevant recipe during the alleged phytase trials added Phyzyme TPT 2500 at a constant 0.4 pound per ton. With respect to phytase, Judge Greaves noted explicitly that "GOMI's contemporaneous feed recipes do not support the claim that Dr. Greenwood varied the dosages," and he separately condemned the Salinomycin claim as "a clear example of the chicken (research credit study) coming before the egg (research)".

This holding illustrates how the Tax Court weighs evidence: the court declined to rely solely on employee testimony that conflicted with contemporaneous feed records, and it refused to base findings solely on alliantgroup's flock determinations when the basis for them was unknown. Furthermore, the court emphasized that technical uncertainty cannot be invented retroactively through hindsight bias merely because a production run experienced disease outbreaks or suboptimal commercial performance; the uncertainty must exist as of the beginning of the research activities in the taxable year for which the credit is claimed, although the regulations do not require any particular type of document to prove it.
Failure 2: Failure to Enforce the Post-Resolution Commercial Cutoff (The HatchPak and Tylan 2013 Disallowance)

A pervasive structural flaw in multi-year R&D claims is the failure to demarcate the exact temporal boundary when technical uncertainty is resolved and commercial production begins. Under the section 174 uncertainty test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) (the court found it unnecessary to reach the IRS's alternative argument under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), which excludes research conducted after the beginning of commercial production), once information objectively available to the taxpayer establishes the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component, subsequent expenditures no longer qualify as research costs.

In the HatchPak and Tylan trial, GOMI evaluated whether combining a hatchery coccidiosis vaccine (HatchPak) with an antibiotic regimen (Tylan) would effectively control coccidiosis while curbing HatchPak's known side effect, necrotic enteritis, under GOMI's standard production process. For taxable year 2012, the Tax Court agreed that objective biological uncertainty existed, validated the experimental broilers as pilot models under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4), and allowed $5,115,281 in feed and supply QREs. However, GOMI also claimed the feed costs of the flocks covered by 20 contracts on all company-related farms that received the same HatchPak and Tylan regimen (combined with Vaxxitek and, for some flocks, Calsporin or Sporulin) in the third and fourth quarters of 2013. The Tax Court disallowed the 2013 QREs in their entirety, holding that "the successful results in 2012 resolved the uncertainty in 2013". Because petitioners claimed the same uncertainty in 2013 as in 2012, GOMI followed the exact same procedure, and its live production manager and veterinarian testified that they expected the regimen to keep working, no section 174 uncertainty existed at the start of the 2013 trials; the court refused to accept the regimen's unexpected 2013 failure as a post hoc justification of uncertainty.
Failure 3: Absence of Granular Accounting Nexus Between Experimental Units and Claimed QREs (The Floramax Failure)

Even where genuine scientific experimentation occurs, a taxpayer must establish a verifiable accounting nexus ("linkage") connecting the qualified experimental activity to the specific supply expenditures claimed under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). In GOMI's probiotic trials, the company tested Floramax (administered via drinking water on select company-related farms to flocks covered by 45 contracts, according to petitioners' representations; the opinion does not quantify the Floramax QREs) before moving sequentially to Sporulin and Calsporin. While the court found that all three probiotic trials, Floramax included, followed a clear scientific progression (forming a hypothesis, administering each probiotic, comparing mortality and feed-conversion metrics against a control group or historic farm data, and moving to the next alternative when results disappointed), and contemporaneous feed recipes recorded the addition of Sporulin and Calsporin to the feed, GOMI's recordkeeping for Floramax collapsed.

Specifically, GOMI failed to retain contemporaneous records identifying which specific broiler flocks and grower houses actually received the Floramax water treatment. Because the primary QRE driver was the cost of the feed consumed by the pilot-model broilers in the treated flocks, the inability to identify the exact treated flocks made it impossible to isolate the qualifying pilot-model feed costs from ordinary commercial feed costs. Refusing to "wing it with an estimate ungrounded in the record," Judge Greaves disallowed the Floramax trial in full. This exposes a critical vulnerability in pilot-model supply claims: if the experimental unit (the specific flock, batch, or production lot) is not tagged in the taxpayer's enterprise resource planning (ERP) or cost-accounting system, the entire supply QRE pool associated with that trial becomes unsubstantiated.
Failure 4: Violation of Annual Tax Accounting Principles (The LT Vaccine Administration Failure)

Federal income taxation operates on a strict annual accounting system (IRC § 441), and the IRC § 41 research credit is an incremental, year-specific calculation that compares current-year QREs against a defined historical base period. Consequently, a taxpayer must prove not only that qualified research occurred, but precisely when the activities and expenditures took place.

In GOMI's Laryngotracheitis (LT) vaccine trials, the company investigated two distinct technical questions: testing alternative physical methods of vaccine administration, and priming broilers at the hatchery with a recombinant vector vaccine to reduce the adverse respiratory side effects of a subsequent chicken embryo origin (CEO) vaccine. While the court allowed the LT Priming trial conducted in 2014 (but only for the six big broiler flocks the record could identify as primed under the September 2, 2014 vaccine protocol, out of 133 contracts claimed)—noting that GOMI's prior experience priming breeders did not resolve uncertainty for broilers because of the drastic differences between the two—the court completely disallowed the LT Method of Administration trial. At trial, GOMI's witnesses could not pinpoint from memory or records whether the method-of-administration trials occurred in taxable year 2012 or taxable year 2013. Because no witness or document established when the trials occurred, the court could not apply the four-part test to any particular tax year (for example, whether uncertainty remained in 2013 if the trials took place in 2012) or allocate the QREs between years, so the entire sub-project failed.
Failure 5: Base-Period Substantiation Collapse, Rejection of the Cohan Rule, and the IRC Section 41(c)(5)(B) Rate Penalty

Perhaps the single most expensive technical failure across the entire litigation was GOMI's inability to substantiate its historical base-period QREs for taxable years 2009, 2010, and 2011 under the ASC method. Under IRC § 41(c)(5)(A), the standard ASC credit equals:
ASC = 0.14 × (QRE<sub>current</sub> − 0.50 × (QRE<sub>t−1</sub> + QRE<sub>t−2</sub> + QRE<sub>t−3</sub>) / 3)

However, under IRC § 41(c)(5)(B), if the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, the credit rate drops to a flat 6% of current-year QREs (ASC = 0.06 × QRE<sub>current</sub>).

The opinion notes that it was unclear whether GOMI lacked the documentation to substantiate its 2009–2011 base-year QREs or whether alliantgroup simply failed to search for it. Instead, to claim the 14% rate, alliantgroup estimated GOMI's 2009–2011 base-period QREs by calculating the average ratio of claimed QREs to total feed expenses during the 2012–2014 credit years (10.23%) and applying that 10.23% ratio to GOMI's total 2009–2011 feed expenses, and petitioners urged the court to accept that estimate under the estimation rule of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930).

The Tax Court flatly rejected this methodology. Reaffirming settled precedent, Judge Greaves held that "we do not apply the Cohan rule to estimate expenses paid or incurred if the taxpayer provides 'no evidence at all that would permit an informed estimate' of the deduction, basis, or other tax advantage". The court added that the study had grossly overvalued the credit-year QREs, which would have lowered the ratio, and that petitioners' evidence for 2009–2011 (brief board-minute references to Hubbard and MX genetic line trials and ventilation improvements, plus testimony about runt and stunt syndrome work in 2010–2012 that could not identify the farms involved or the size of the experimental groups) gave no basis for an informed estimate, so an extrapolation from 2012–2014 credit ratios lacked any factual anchor. Consequently, the court concluded that GOMI had no QREs for 2009, 2010, and 2011 and enforced the statutory start-up limitation under IRC § 41(c)(5)(B), slashing the credit rate from 14% to 6% on all surviving trials.
Failure 6: Business Component Framing, Pilot Model Boundaries, and Statutory Exclusions (Adaptation and Funded Research Dynamics)

While GOMI suffered severe losses on substantiation, it survived the IRS's structural legal challenges regarding business component classification and statutory exclusions—battles that highlight acute traps for taxpayers in manufacturing, agriculture, and contract engineering. Initially, inconsistencies in the record about how petitioners described the business components allowed the IRS to argue, relying on IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Union Carbide rather than United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), which the opinion does not cite, that GOMI was merely trying to improve its process of raising chickens to reduce grow-out costs, rather than developing a product. Under Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), which the George opinion applies to hold that QREs for a process-only trial exclude the costs the taxpayer would have incurred to make the same product by the standard method (the opinion does not cite the separate J.G. Boswell Co. v. Commissioner litigation, Docket No. 2408-19), classifying the business component as a process would have jeopardized the entire roughly $63 million supply QRE pool. GOMI overcame this because petitioners stipulated, and the court found from the aim of each trial, that the objective was to improve the health and quality of the broiler itself rather than to cut costs or increase output (creating a healthier, more uniform product), thereby qualifying the birds as physical "pilot models" under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4).

Similarly, the IRS contended that any GOMI project aimed at uniform bird weights merely adapted an existing product to customer size requirements under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B). The Tax Court rejected this broad reading, holding that "adaptation" in its ordinary statutory sense excludes only minor alterations of an existing design, whereas the improved poultry product was a business component distinct from GOMI's standard broiler and the coccidiosis control GOMI hypothesized represented a "magnitude of change greater than minor alterations". Finally, in vertically integrated production and commercial contracting, taxpayers frequently utilize third-party contract growers, vendor-sponsored input trials, or customer specification agreements. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), research is disqualified as "funded" if the taxpayer fails either the payment-contingency prong (payment must be contingent on the technical success of the research) or the substantial-rights prong (the taxpayer must retain substantial rights in the research results). As reinforced by the Eighth Circuit in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024) and the Tax Court in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, courts parse intellectual property clauses, risk-of-loss provisions, and vendor or customer contracts project by project. In George, the IRS did not raise, and the court did not decide, the funded research exclusion; the record simply showed that GOMI retained ownership of the broilers and supplied the feed and medications to independent contract growers (who were paid under a tournament-style performance system), facts consistent with treating the flocks as GOMI's own pilot models rather than research funded by vendors or growers.
3. Comparative Summary Table
Mapping Statutory Requirements Against Taxpayer Failures and Judicial Standards of Proof

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement adjudicated in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, against the specific deficiencies in GOMI's claim and the evidentiary standard of proof enforced by the U.S. Tax Court.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure or Litigation Vulnerability
Tax Court's Standard of Proof & Legal Holding

cells: Technical Uncertainty & Ex-Ante Intent IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); IRC § 174; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)

Claimed dosage experimentation (Salinomycin, Phytase) that contemporaneous feed recipes did not corroborate; attempted to infer 2013 HatchPak and Tylan uncertainty from that year's unexpected failure.

Uncertainty must objectively exist at the outset of the activity, not invented in hindsight. However, vendor testing in sterile labs does not eliminate uncertainty regarding commercial-scale biological performance.
Post-Resolution Commercial Cutoff IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); IRC § 174; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) (the IRS's § 41(d)(4)(A) argument was not reached)
Continued claiming feed supply QREs in 2013 for the HatchPak and Tylan vaccine/antibiotic protocol after 2012 trials proved its commercial efficacy.

Once experimental results resolve the underlying technical uncertainty, a later identical trial lacks section 174 uncertainty, and a subsequent unexpected failure cannot supply it after the fact, cutting off QRE eligibility.
Business Component Classification (Product vs. Process) IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii); IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)

The record described the business components inconsistently (petitioners ultimately stipulated to an improved poultry product), exposing the claim to an IRS process challenge under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Union Carbide that would disqualify ordinary production supply costs.

The court looks to the functional objective of the trials: if the research aims to improve physical quality, uniformity, and disease resistance of the output rather than mere process efficiency, the business component is a product ("improved poultry product").
Pilot Model Qualification & Supply QRE Nexus IRC § 41(b)(2)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)

Claimed roughly $63M in feed supply QREs without wage QREs; in the Floramax trial (QREs not quantified in the opinion), failed to maintain records showing which specific broiler flocks received the additive.

Live biological outputs raised to evaluate product viability qualify as "pilot models," making their feed a valid supply QRE even if zero wage QREs are claimed. However, the taxpayer must prove via contemporaneous records exactly which experimental units received the treatment; courts will not estimate ungrounded flock allocations.
Process of Experimentation IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)

Relied on employee testimony and the credit study claiming dosage variations (Salinomycin, Phytase; QREs not quantified in the opinion) that were directly refuted by contemporaneous feed mill recipes showing static dosages (e.g., 0.4 lbs/ton).

A valid process of experimentation requires contemporaneous proof of hypothesis formulation, systematic testing of alternatives, and data analysis (Ross 708, Sporulin/Calsporin). Overlapping commercial variables do not disqualify field trials, but the court declined to credit testimony and study conclusions that contemporaneous records contradicted or could not corroborate.
Annual Tax Accounting & Temporal Substantiation IRC § 41(a); IRC § 441; IRC § 6001
In the LT Vaccine Method of Administration trial, witnesses could not establish whether the experimental trials occurred in taxable year 2012 or 2013.

Because IRC § 41 is an annual, incremental calculation, taxpayers must substantiate the exact taxable year in which qualified activities and QREs occurred; temporal ambiguity mandates complete disallowance.
ASC Base-Period Substantiation & Cohan Estimation IRC § 41(c)(5)(A)–(B); Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)
Offered no project-level records for the 2009–2011 base years; attempted to estimate base-period QREs by applying a 10.23% ratio derived from 2012–2014 credit years.

The Cohan rule cannot be used to estimate base-period QREs where the taxpayer provides "no evidence at all that would permit an informed estimate". Unsubstantiated base periods trigger the IRC § 41(c)(5)(B) start-up rule, slashing the ASC rate from 14% to 6%.
Statutory Exclusions (Adaptation & Funded Research) IRC § 41(d)(4)(B); IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)
IRS asserted that controlling bird uniformity for buyers was a customer "adaptation" and that the trials were routine testing or quality control; the funded research exclusion was not raised.

"Adaptation" under § 41(d)(4)(B) bars only minor alterations of an existing design, not substantial biological/product changes. Under § 41(d)(4)(H), the taxpayer must bear financial risk of experimental failure and retain substantial rights to the research (an exclusion not at issue in George).
Accuracy-Related Penalties & Reasonable Cause IRC § 6662(a); IRC § 6664(c)

The IRS disallowed the credits in full and asserted 20% negligence penalties for 2014 and 2016 (alternatively, substantial understatement for 2016); the court ultimately disallowed over 80% of the claimed credits.

Penalties are abated under § 6664(c) where the taxpayer proves good-faith reliance on a reputable adviser, provides full access to corporate books and records, and receives a comprehensive technical study (two reports totaling nearly 100 pages).

body.text: Project-by-Project Adjudication Matrix in George v. Commissioner

To illustrate how the Tax Court applied these evidentiary standards to GOMI's operations, the table below details the disposition of the trials evaluated in the opinion, with the probiotic trial split into its Floramax and Sporulin/Calsporin components (the Vaxxitek low-dosage IBD trial, which the court disallowed in full because nothing in the record identified the experimental flocks or the dosages given, has no separate row).

cells: 1. Salinomycin (Coccidiostat Feed Additive)
Testing higher dosages combined with chemical coccidiostats (such as Robenz) to improve coccidiosis control.
Petitioners claimed higher dosages, but contemporaneous feed recipes showed the same dosages as prior years, and Robenz appeared in only one April 3, 2012 recipe not linked to the remaining flocks.
Disallowed in Full (QREs not quantified in the opinion). Classic example of "the chicken (credit study) coming before the egg (research)".
2. Phytase (Digestive Enzyme Additive)
Varying enzyme dosages to determine an optimal nutrient absorption matrix.
Contemporaneous feed recipes proved Dr. Greenwood used a constant dosage of 0.4 lbs/ton in every relevant recipe during the alleged trials, within the same 0.3 to 0.5 lbs/ton range used since 2010.
Disallowed in Full. Operational records directly refuted the consultant study's narrative of systematic trial-and-error.
3. HatchPak & Tylan (Vaccine & Antibiotic Regimen)
Evaluating whether a combined hatchery vaccine and antibiotic program could control disease in commercial grow-out houses.

Both experts agreed vendor lab research did not resolve 2012 uncertainty, and 800-series feed recipes and settlement data identified the 14 trial flocks; 2012 data showed the regimen succeeded, and GOMI continued using it in 2013.
Allowed for 2012 ($5,115,281 QREs); Disallowed for 2013. 2012 success eliminated technical uncertainty; the identical 2013 trials lacked section 174 uncertainty.
4. Floramax (Water-Administered Probiotic)
Testing whether a water-administered probiotic used mainly in turkeys would improve broiler gut health, on flocks covered by 45 contracts per petitioners.
GOMI lacked contemporaneous logs identifying which specific broiler flocks received the additive.
Disallowed in Full (QREs not quantified in the opinion). Court refused to "wing it with an estimate ungrounded in the record" or rely on alliantgroup's unexplained flock determinations.
5. Sporulin & Calsporin (Feed Probiotics)
Sequential testing of alternative probiotic strains to replace antibiotics and reduce mortality.

Contemporaneous feed recipes recorded each probiotic's addition; the record showed a hypothesis, comparison with historic farm data, and an iterative pivot to the next product (Sporulin showed no improvement and Calsporin results were inconclusive).
Allowed in Full. QREs of $4,748,616 (Sporulin) and $2,531,962 (Calsporin) allowed for 2013; the court found the probiotic process of experimentation "far exceeds a simple evaluation of alternatives".
6. LT Vaccines (Administration vs. Vector Priming)

(a) Testing alternative administration methods; (b) Priming broilers with vector vaccine to reduce side effects of CEO vaccine (administered at the hatchery; Vaxxitek, an IBD vaccine, was a separate trial).

Witnesses could not recall if administration trials occurred in 2012 or 2013. Priming trials were supported by a September 2, 2014 vaccine protocol and settlement data; prior breeder use did not resolve broiler physiology questions.

Mixed Holding: Administration Method Disallowed (no tax year could be established for the trials); Vector Priming Allowed (valid biological uncertainty and experimentation, but only for six big broiler contracts in 2014, yielding $1,521,039 in QREs).
7. Ross 708 Genetics (Broiler Genetic Line)
Testing Ross 708 genetic broiler line against the standard Cobb 500 line to improve yield, uniformity, and feed conversion.
Contemporaneous hypothesis, Cobb 500 control houses on the same farm, distinct genetic line codes in settlement data, and University of Arkansas yield analysis followed by margin analysis.
Allowed in Full ($398,520 QREs). Praised by the court as "the cleanest example of the scientific method presented in these cases".

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the holdings of George v. Commissioner into actionable tax governance, the following two applied case studies examine high-exposure taxpayers facing the exact legal, technical, contractual, and accounting pitfalls identified by Judge Greaves. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial architecture designed to withstand IRS examination and satisfy modern substantiation mandates, including the business-component reporting requirements of Form 6765 (Section G) and the interplay between IRC § 41 and IRC § 174/174A capitalization rules.
Case Study 1: Vertically Integrated Commercial Swine and Feed Producer (Heartland BioPork Corp.)
Industry Scenario and Exposure to George v. Commissioner Pitfalls

Heartland BioPork Corp. ("Heartland") is a vertically integrated commercial swine producer operating feed mills, breeding facilities, and 120 contract grow-out barns across the Midwest. Seeking to eliminate sub-therapeutic antibiotics while maintaining carcass lean-meat uniformity and suppressing porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS), Heartland's veterinary and nutrition teams conduct commercial-scale trials involving custom-formulated phytogenic essential-oil feed matrices, water-soluble bacteriophage treatments, and a Duroc-cross terminal genetic sire line. Heartland spends $18 million annually on feed and biological supplies for barns involved in these initiatives.

Heartland faces four acute vulnerabilities mirroring GOMI's failures in George v. Commissioner. First, regarding the Salinomycin and Phytase contradiction risk, Heartland's nutritionists verbally inform tax advisors that they varied essential-oil inclusion rates from 0.2 to 0.8 pounds per ton across the year, whereas the automated feed mill batching system defaults to a static standard master recipe unless manually overridden and logged. Second, mirroring the Floramax commingling failure, bacteriophage treatments are delivered via portable water-medicator pumps rotated among 35 contract grower barns without logging the specific lot numbers of the swine herds receiving the water treatment in Heartland's ERP system. Third, replicating the HatchPak and Tylan 2013 cutoff error, a 2025 PRRS vaccine-priming protocol succeeded in the fourth quarter of 2025, and Heartland rolled the protocol out across 60 barns in 2026 while continuing to code all 2026 feed costs in those barns as PRRS Trial QREs. Fourth, creating contractual and vendor funding exposure, a European biotechnology vendor supplies the experimental bacteriophage at a 50% discount in exchange for Heartland sharing raw necropsy and mortality data, while Heartland's contract grower agreements pay growers a base fee plus a feed-conversion bonus, raising IRS questions regarding whether the research is "funded" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) or whether the hogs are process inputs rather than Heartland's "pilot models" under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4).
Step-by-Step Remediation Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance (Stage-Gate Uncertainty and Commercial Cutoff Controls)

To eliminate the "chicken before the egg" retrospective study trap and enforce the HatchPak and Tylan resolved-uncertainty rule, Heartland must replace annual post-hoc tax interviews with a mandatory Pre-Trial Scientific Charter and Stage-Gate Governance Protocol. Under Gate 0 of this protocol (the Ex-Ante Uncertainty and Business Component Charter), before any experimental feed batch is mixed or any biological treatment is administered, the Lead Veterinarian or Nutritionist must execute a digital, timestamped Trial Initiation Charter mapped directly to Form 6765 Section G business-component fields. The Charter must explicitly define the business component as a product—an Improved Commercial Market Hog under a specific treatment or genetic line—rather than a production process. Furthermore, it must articulate the exact biological uncertainty regarding capability, method, or design and include a Vendor Lab Translation Memo explaining why the vendor's sterile laboratory efficacy studies do not resolve uncertainty within Heartland's multi-variable commercial barn environments, specifically citing microbial loads, stocking density, and seasonal thermal stress.

Once a trial is underway, Gate 1 (the Iterative Protocol Modification Log) requires that every dosage or formulation change be authorized through a formal Nutritional Change Order prior to physical implementation at the feed mill. At the conclusion of each grow-out cycle, when hogs reach market weight and slaughter data is analyzed, Gate 2 (Formal Uncertainty Resolution and Commercial Cutoff Sign-Off) requires a Trial Closeout Committee comprising the Vice President of Live Production, the Lead Veterinarian, and the Tax Director to review the necropsy and slaughter uniformity data. If the hypothesis is validated and the protocol is approved for standard commercial rollout, the Committee executes a Commercial Release Certificate. This certificate immediately terminates the R&D project code in the ERP system, preventing subsequent commercial feed expenditures from contaminating future-year QRE claims and avoiding the HatchPak and Tylan 2013 disallowance. Conversely, if a second-year trial is required—such as testing summer heat-stress interactions against winter baseline conditions—a new Gate 0 Charter must document the distinct, unresolved environmental uncertainty before 2026 costs can be captured.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Technical Documentation Architecture (Automated Mill-to-Field Reconciliation)

To prevent the fatal Salinomycin and Phytase failure—where oral claims of dosage testing were destroyed by static feed mill records—Heartland must integrate its technical documentation directly with its operational manufacturing systems. Heartland must configure its computerized feed mill batching software so that no experimental trial can be claimed unless a distinct Experimental Ration Code is generated in the mill's Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) database for each test level and control group. The actual automated scale weight tickets from the mill mixer showing the exact pounds per ton of essential oil added to each truckload must be automatically archived into the R&D substantiation repository.

To enforce this architecture, Heartland's tax governance policy must strictly prohibit the inclusion of any project in the IRC § 41 calculation based solely on oral testimony. Before any trial is reported on Form 6765, the internal tax team must perform a complete reconciliation verifying that the feed mill PLC batch logs show actual physical variance in additive dosages across test and control rations matching the Gate 0 Charter. Additionally, following the Ross 708 gold standard ("the cleanest example of the scientific method") and the LT Vaccine Priming physiological distinction rule, Heartland's technical files must pair each experimental barn with a designated contemporaneous control barn, or document why overlapping commercial variables were intentionally integrated into the commercial test design. Whenever an additive or vaccine was previously administered to breeding sows, the technical file must include a veterinary anatomical analysis documenting why physiological and metabolic differences between multi-parity breeding sows and rapid-growth market hogs create brand-new dosage and immune-response uncertainties.
Step 3: Engineering Contract Terms (Vendor Trial Agreements and Contract Grower Structures)

To insulate its $18 million pilot-model feed supply pool from the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion, the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion, and Union Carbide-style process challenges under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), Heartland must execute three targeted contractual reforms. First, Heartland's Master Grower Contracts must explicitly stipulate that the arrangement is a livestock bailment in which Heartland retains 100% legal title to the swine herds, the experimental feed, and the veterinary supplies at all times during grow-out. The contract must specify that for designated Experimental Pilot-Model Herds, the contract grower is compensated on a fixed square-footage facility fee rather than a mortality or feed-conversion penalty structure, ensuring that Heartland bears 100% of the financial risk if an experimental ration causes growth stunting or elevated mortality.

Second, to prevent the IRS from arguing that the European biotech vendor's 50% price discount on bacteriophages renders Heartland's trials "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), Heartland must revise the vendor purchase agreement. The contractual addendum must establish that Heartland is purchasing the bacteriophage at a commercial volume discount with zero reimbursement or price rebate contingent on trial outcomes, that Heartland retains exclusive ownership and substantial rights in its findings without granting a royalty-free license back to the vendor to commercialize Heartland's proprietary dosing matrix, and that any anonymized performance data shared with the vendor does not restrict Heartland from utilizing its discovered nutritional and veterinary protocols across its own operations or licensing them to third parties. Third, to preempt an IRS adaptation exclusion argument under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), Heartland's supply agreements with downstream meatpackers must frame carcass lean-meat and antibiotic-free specifications as general market grade standards rather than custom engineering for a single buyer, while internal charters document that achieving those biological traits required fundamental genetic and microbiome redesigns constituting "a magnitude of change greater than minor alterations".
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and QRE Cost Accounting Systems

To eliminate the Floramax flock-tracking failure, the LT Vaccine annual accounting failure, and the Cohan base-period penalty, Heartland must deploy a granular ERP sub-ledger tracking architecture. Every experimental herd placed in a grow-out barn must be assigned a unique Pilot-Model Herd Identification Code in Heartland's ERP system. When feed trucks deliver rations or veterinary technicians install water-medicator pumps, the delivery bill of lading and barn log must scan that specific Pilot-Model Herd Identification Code. Only feed actually delivered to and consumed by verified experimental herds during the active Gate 0 through Gate 2 window may be posted to the General Ledger QRE Supply sub-account, with a mandatory closeout reconciliation between feed delivered to the farm and feed actually consumed by the animals.

For grow-out trials that straddle December 31—such as herds placed on November 15, 2025, and slaughtered on March 10, 2026—Heartland's ERP system must generate an automated December 31 inventory and feed-consumption cutoff report. This procedure isolates the exact feed tonnage consumed between November 15 and December 31, 2025 (claimed on the 2025 Form 6765) from feed tonnage consumed between January 1 and March 10, 2026 (claimed on the 2026 Form 6765), completely eliminating the LT Vaccine Method of Administration temporal ambiguity. Finally, to guarantee the 14% ASC rate under IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) and avoid the 6% start-up penalty of § 41(c)(5)(B), Heartland must maintain a rolling four-year Contemporaneous Base-Year Substantiation Vault containing the exact PLC feed mill logs, herd identification codes, and trial closeout reports for each of the three preceding taxable years. If Heartland must reconstruct any historical base year where granular herd tags were incomplete, it cannot use a top-down credit-year ratio like the rejected 10.23% GOMI method; instead, it must compile actual historical feed mill batch tickets and veterinary necropsy invoices from those specific base years to establish a conservative, factually anchored floor of proven base-year QREs that does not rely on ungrounded Cohan estimates.
Case Study 2: Specialty Industrial Polymer and Catalyst Manufacturer (Apex Elastomers LLC)
Industry Scenario and Exposure to George v. Commissioner Pitfalls

Apex Elastomers LLC ("Apex") is a middle-market specialty chemical and industrial polymer manufacturer that produces high-temperature fluoroelastomer seals and custom catalyst substrates on continuous commercial extrusion and curing lines. Because laboratory bench-scale reactors (2-liter vessels) cannot replicate the shear stress, thermal gradients, and residence-time distribution of Apex's 5,000-pound-per-hour commercial twin-screw extruders, Apex performs full-scale commercial plant trials to develop new peroxide-cured elastomer formulations and custom aerospace seals for original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). Apex claims $6.5 million annually in raw polymer and curing-agent supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) alongside $1.5 million in engineering wage QREs.

As the legal analysis of George v. Commissioner demonstrates, a manufacturer that cannot connect commercial production runs to a defined experimental protocol faces the exact same disallowance framework as an agricultural producer. Specifically, Apex faces five critical pitfalls identified in George. First, exhibiting hindsight bias on failed production runs, whenever a standard commercial extrusion run suffers scorching, premature cross-linking, or off-spec tensile strength, Apex's plant manager retroactively reclassifies the scrapped $150,000 raw material batch as an R&D Trial at year-end without any pre-run experimental protocol. Second, mirroring the Salinomycin and Phytase contradiction between R&D narratives and operational logs, Apex's R&D credit consultant drafts narratives claiming engineers systematically varied extruder barrel temperatures and peroxide catalyst ratios during the second quarter, whereas the plant's automated Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) historian shows the extruder ran at standard fixed setpoints of 185°C and 1.2% peroxide.

Third, creating acute process-versus-product misclassification and pilot model disqualification exposure, Apex's internal documentation describes its plant trials as Continuous Extrusion Process Optimization, inviting the IRS to argue under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Union Carbide that the business component is the extrusion process rather than the elastomer product, which would disqualify the $6.5 million in raw polymer supplies consumed during the runs. Fourth, triggering contractual adaptation and funded research traps, Apex enters into fixed-price purchase orders with aerospace OEMs to modify seal geometries and thermal tolerances using boilerplate OEM terms that vest all intellectual property, test data, and design rights in the OEM, implicating both the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion and the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion under Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith v. Commissioner. Fifth, suffering from missing base-period documentation, Apex acquired a chemical division in 2024 whose 2023–2025 historical R&D records were stored only as summary journal entries, threatening a reduction from the 14% ASC rate to 6% under IRC § 41(c)(5)(B).
Step-by-Step Remediation Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance (Pre-Run Design of Experiments and Hindsight-Bias Prevention)

To eradicate hindsight bias—where failed production runs are retroactively disguised as R&D—and to segregate product pilot models from process optimization, Apex must institute a Commercial-Line R&D Authorization Framework. Under Apex's revised governance rules, no commercial-line production run may be classified as qualified research unless the Polymer R&D Director issues a formal Commercial-Scale Design of Experiments (DOE) Ticket in the Manufacturing Execution System (MES) at least 24 hours prior to raw material staging. Any standard commercial batch that unexpectedly fails quality control is strictly routed to a non-qualifying Cost of Scrap or Quality Control account, and retrospective reclassification of failed commercial runs is prohibited.

Simultaneously, to protect its $6.5 million supply QRE claim from IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Union Carbide challenges, Apex's governance committee must strictly separate projects into two distinct statutory tracks on Form 6765 Section G. Under Track A (Product Business Component and Pilot Model Lots), where the technical uncertainty concerns the chemical formulation, cross-link density, or physical specification of a new or improved elastomer compound, the business component is formally classified as a Product. The experimental commercial batch is designated in advance as a Pilot Model Lot under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4), constructed solely to resolve scale-up formulation uncertainty that the 2-liter laboratory reactor could not resolve. Under the reasoning of George, the raw monomer, filler, and curing supplies actually consumed in constructing that Pilot Model Lot (net of shrink, scrap allowances, and allocated overhead, mirroring the adjustments the court accepted for GOMI's feed) can qualify as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). Under Track B (Process Business Component), where the chemical formulation of the elastomer is already established and engineers are solely testing screw-speed kinematics to reduce electricity costs on standard commercial orders, the business component is classified as a Process. For Track B projects, Apex claims only the qualified engineering wages and incremental destructive testing supplies, intentionally excluding standard commercial raw materials that would have been produced and sold absent the process test.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Technical Documentation Architecture (SCADA and MES Telemetry Synchronization)

To prevent the Salinomycin and Phytase failure—where consultant narratives contradicted operational logs—and to replicate the structured scientific method praised in Sporulin and Calsporin and Ross 708, Apex must link its engineering narratives directly to automated machine telemetry. Whenever a Commercial-Scale DOE Ticket is executed on the twin-screw extruder, the MES software must automatically extract the time-series SCADA log showing the exact parameter variations executed during the run—such as stepping peroxide concentration from 1.1% at 175°C to 1.45% at 190°C, followed by a co-agent shift at 182°C—and cryptographically attach that telemetry export to the DOE Ticket.

Mirroring GOMI's successful Sporulin and Calsporin substantiation, Apex's R&D documentation portal must enforce a sequential chain-of-evidence structure linking the initial hypothesis in the first DOE ticket to the post-run rheometer and tensile laboratory test data demonstrating failure, followed by the engineering root-cause analysis memorandum and the subsequent iterative hypothesis pivot in the next DOE ticket. This contemporaneous sequence proves to the IRS and the Tax Court that the plant trials followed a disciplined scientific method rather than ad-hoc plant troubleshooting. Once a compound formulation passes post-extrusion rheometer, thermal aging, and tensile testing, the R&D Director must execute a First Article Formulation Freeze. Any subsequent production batches of that compound are automatically routed to standard commercial manufacturing, preventing a HatchPak and Tylan post-resolution disallowance.
Step 3: Engineering Contract Terms (Defeating Adaptation and Funded Research Exclusions)

To ensure that OEM customer collaborations are not disqualified under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) (adaptation) or IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) (funded research), Apex must overhaul its commercial legal templates. In Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, the Tax Court emphasized that it parses intellectual property, copyright, license, and confidentiality clauses project by project rather than treating them as boilerplate. Consequently, Apex must strike any OEM purchase-order clause granting the customer all right, title, and interest in and to developmental data, formulas, and inventions. In its place, Apex must insert a Bifurcated Intellectual Property Clause stipulating that while the customer owns title solely to the physical finished seal hardware delivered under the order, Apex retains sole and exclusive ownership—or at minimum a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free right to use, exploit, and commercialize—all underlying chemical formulations, polymer compounding matrices, curing kinematics, and process discoveries developed during performance of the agreement across any other customer or commercial application without restriction.

To satisfy the payment-contingency prong of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) and overcome the Eighth Circuit's holding in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), Apex's custom development contracts must be structured as fixed-price deliverables where payment is explicitly contingent on the Pilot Model Lot passing objective, uncertain technical performance thresholds (such as passing 1,000-hour sour-gas rapid decompression testing at 230°C under ASTM standards), with Apex bearing the full contractual obligation to refund advances and absorb all raw material and engineering costs if the technical specification cannot be achieved. Furthermore, to defeat the adaptation exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), every Gate 0 DOE Ticket for an OEM-initiated seal project must include a Baseline Incompatibility Analysis documenting why Apex's existing commercial polymer library chemically degrades under the new thermal or chemical environment, proving that the project requires synthesizing a fundamentally new cross-linking architecture representing "a magnitude of change greater than minor alterations" under the George standard.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Annual Cutoffs, and Base-Period Reconstruction

To prevent the Floramax unlinked-supply disallowance, the LT Vaccine annual accounting violation, and the Cohan base-period rate reduction, Apex must implement three strict cost-accounting controls. First, raw polymers and curing agents issued from warehouse inventory for a Track A Pilot Model Lot must be scanned via barcode directly to the specific DOE Work Order Number. Unlike GOMI's unsubstantiated Floramax allocations, this creates an immutable audit trail linking every pound of raw material from the vendor invoice to the specific experimental extrusion batch. To ensure proper statutory coordination between IRC § 41 and IRC § 174/174A—including the required IRC § 280C(c) election or § 174A deduction reduction—all pilot-model supply costs must be mapped in real time to dedicated § 174 and § 41 general ledger accounts.

Second, engineers and compounding technicians must log hours weekly to specific DOE Work Order Numbers tied to exact calendar dates. For multi-phase polymer trials spanning December 31, the ERP system must automatically close Phase 1 work orders at midnight on December 31 and open Phase 2 work orders on January 1, ensuring strict compliance with IRC § 41 annual accounting principles. Third, to substantiate the 2023–2025 base years of its newly acquired division without falling into the Cohan trap, Apex must not estimate historical QREs using a percentage ratio derived from its 2026 credit study. Instead, Apex must perform a forensic archival extraction of the acquired division's 2023–2025 laboratory notebooks, SCADA historian backups, quality-assurance rheometer logs, and W-2 wage registers for dedicated R&D chemists. By anchoring the 2023–2025 base period in verifiable contemporaneous records—even if conservative in total dollar amount—Apex establishes the factual foundation required by the Tax Court, preserving the full 14% ASC rate under IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) while maintaining complete documentation of its external tax advisor's review to secure penalty protection under IRC § 6664(c).
5. Synthesis of Strategic Implications for U.S. Taxpayers

The Tax Court's decision in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10, fundamentally recalibrates the risk profile of federal R&D tax credit claims across the United States. On the substantive law, the opinion provides an expansive, taxpayer-favorable interpretation of IRC § 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4): it confirms that commercial-scale trials in non-traditional, biologically or operationally complex industries can satisfy the four-part test, validates live biological and commercial-scale outputs as "pilot models" whose developmental feed and raw material inputs qualify as supply QREs, affirms that taxpayers may selectively claim supply QREs without claiming wage QREs, and restricts the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion to minor design alterations.

Simultaneously, however, the ruling exposes the fatal structural flaws of the traditional retrospective R&D study model built on post-hoc employee interviews and top-down accounting estimates. When operational records—such as automated feed recipes, SCADA logs, or batch tickets—fail to show actual parameter variations, or when accounting systems cannot trace supplies to specific experimental units and specific taxable years, the Tax Court will disallow the claims regardless of how persuasive the consultant's narrative appears. Moreover, the court's refusal to apply the Cohan rule to ungrounded base-period ratios demonstrates that historical recordkeeping for the three preceding base years is just as critical as current-year documentation if a taxpayer wishes to avoid a mandatory 57% reduction in its ASC credit rate (from 14% down to 6%) under IRC § 41(c)(5)(B). While engaging a reputable advisory firm and granting full data access can shield a taxpayer from 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 and § 6664(c), only real-time, project-level technical and accounting substantiation can preserve the underlying tax credit.
